title: Numerical analysis of physics-informed neural networks and related models in physics-informed machine learning
affiliations: Seminar for Applied Mathematics, ETH Zürich, Switzerland (De Ryck); Seminar for Applied Mathematics & ETH AI Center, ETH Zürich, Switzerland (Mishra)
subdomain: numerical analysis of PINNs: approximation, stability, generalization and training-error theory for forward/inverse PDE problems and operator learning
industry_context: No industry partner named; motivations include astrophysics, climate dynamics, meteorology, nuclear engineering and medical imaging (radiative transfer, pp. 675-676) and finance via Black-Scholes/Kolmogorov PDEs; otherwise academic mathematics (ETH Zürich)
physics_enforced_exact: Abstract PDE L[u]=f, B[u]=g (2.1) enforced through its residual; worked examples: semilinear heat equation u_t = Δu + f(u) with IC u(x,0)=u_0(x) and zero Dirichlet BC (2.6); incompressible Navier-Stokes u_t + u·∇u + ∇p = νΔu, div(u)=0, u(t=0)=u_0 on the d-dimensional torus with periodic BCs (2.8); viscous scalar conservation law u_t + f(u)_x = ν u_xx (2.9) and inviscid u_t + f(u)_x = 0 (2.10); Poisson's equation −Δu = f (2.11); stationary Stokes Δu + ∇p = f, div(u) = f_d (2.17); radiative transfer equation (linear integro-differential, 5.8); Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation (5.25); linear Kolmogorov PDEs incl. heat and Black-Scholes (4.21); nonlinear parabolic Allen-Cahn-type ∂_t u − Δ_x u − F(u) = 0 (4.23)
pde_type: multiple (parabolic heat/Kolmogorov/Allen-Cahn, elliptic Poisson/Stokes, hyperbolic conservation laws, mixed integro-differential radiative transfer)
dimensionality: general d-dimensional theory; illustrative experiments 1D (heat, advection, Poisson) and 2D (Navier-Stokes Taylor-Green vortex); high-dimensional analysed explicitly (Kolmogorov PDEs, parametric heat eq. with parameter dimension d up to very large values, Fig 6.3)
nonlinearity: mixed: linear (Poisson, heat, advection, Kolmogorov, Stokes) to strongly nonlinear (semilinear heat with globally Lipschitz source, incompressible Navier-Stokes convection, scalar conservation laws developing shocks, Allen-Cahn polynomial reaction)
bcs_ic_handled: spatial boundary residual R_s[u_θ](x) = D^k_x u_θ(x) − g(x) (2.42) and temporal/initial residual R_t[u_θ](x) = u_θ(x,0) − u_0(x) (2.43) added to the loss with weights λ_s, λ_t (soft boundary conditions); hard BCs by construction (output transforms: multiply by η(x) with η|∂Ω=0, or subtract u_θ(π)) analysed in §7.5.2; weak/variational losses add boundary terms; inverse (data-assimilation) problems use a data residual R_d[u_θ](x) = Ψ[u_θ](x) − g(x) on an observation subdomain Ω′ (2.47), Ψ possibly interior-only (heat-transfer sensor argument, p. 639)
enforcement_mechanism: soft-penalty on the strong-form PDE residual as the base framework; survey additionally analyses weak/variational enforcement (VPINN test functions, wPINN Kruzhkov entropy residual, deep Ritz energy minimization) and hard constraints; overall framing is an error-decomposition theory for whichever mechanism is chosen
enforcement_details: physics enters as autodiff residual R_PDE[u_θ](z) = L[u_θ](z) − f(z) evaluated at quadrature points; the integral loss is discretized by a quadrature rule chosen by dimension: midpoint/Gauss grids for d ≤ 4, Sobol/Halton low-discrepancy sequences for 4 < d ≤ 20, i.i.d. Monte Carlo for d > 20, giving J(θ,S) = Q^Ω R_PDE² + λ_s Q^∂Ω R_s² + λ_t Q^D R_t² (2.68); weak variants: E_VPIL = Σ_k (∫ u_θ L*[ψ_k] − ∫ f ψ_k)² with K test functions (VPINN) and E_wPIL = max_ψ (∫ u_θ L*[ψ] − ∫ f ψ)² (wPINN), with the Kruzhkov entropy residual R(v,φ,c) = −∫∫(|u−c|φ_t + Q[u;c]φ_x) enforcing entropy admissibility for conservation laws (2.55); variational: minimize E_DRM = I[u_θ] + λ∫(B[u_θ]−g)² (deep Ritz, 2.64); training analysed through the matrix A = <Lφ_i, Lφ_j> + λ<φ_i,φ_j> and operator A∘TT* (Hermitian square L*L composed with tangent-kernel integral operator) whose condition number governs gradient-descent speed
network_architecture: survey of ansatz spaces: MLPs f_θ = σ∘C_L∘…∘σ∘C_0 (2.22); DeepONet G_θ[v](y) = τ_θ(y) + Σ_{k=1}^p β_k(v)τ_k(y) branch/trunk (2.28); general neural operators u ↦ Q∘L_L∘…∘L_1∘R (2.31); FNO with Fourier layers L_ℓ(v)(x) = σ(W_ℓv + b_ℓ + F^{-1}(P_ℓ(k)·F(v))(x)) (2.36); representation-equivariant neural operators (ReNOs); Gaussian processes; linear models (Fourier features, spectral, FEM, RBF, random-feature models/ELM); the conditioning experiments use Fourier-feature models and an FF-MLP u_θ = Φ_θ(Σ_k α_k φ_k(x)) coupling an MLP with rescaled Fourier features
activation_function: discusses Heaviside, logistic, tanh, ReLU/leaky ReLU, softplus; approximation theory (Theorems 4.4, 4.16-4.18) and the numerical examples are centered on tanh networks (softplus for Barron-space results, Theorem 4.29)
input_representation: spatio-temporal coordinates (x,t) or z for PINNs; M sensor locations/values {u(x_j)} for DeepONet branch; input functions v (initial condition u_0, source f, parameter a) for operator learning; Fourier features φ_k(x) for linear models
output_representation: solution field u_θ (with pressure p_θ for Navier-Stokes); operator approximations G_θ[v]; output transforms for hard BCs (e.g. η(x)u_θ(x) or u_θ(x) − u_θ(π))
loss_terms: E_PIL[u_θ]² = ∫_{D×[0,T]} R_PDE² + λ_s∫_{∂D×[0,T]} R_s² + λ_t∫_0^T R_t² (2.46); discretized training loss J(θ,S) = (1/N_i)Σ(L[u_θ](z_i)−f(z_i))² + (λ_s/N_s)Σ(u_θ(y_i)−u(y_i))² + (λ_t/N_t)Σ(u_θ(x_i,0)−u(x_i,0))² (2.68); optional data term λ_d∫R_d² and parameter regularization λ_r||θ||₂² (2.48); weak losses (2.50)-(2.51) and entropy-residual loss (2.55)-(2.56) for wPINN; variational deep-Ritz loss (2.64)
loss_weighting: fixed hyperparameters λ_s, λ_t in the base formulation; §7.5.1 compares three principled choices via condition-number analysis: optimal λ* = argmin_λ κ(A_λ) (7.33), learning-rate annealing λ*_a = max_k|(∇_θ R(θ))_k| / ((2K+1)^{-1}Σ_k|(∇_θ B(θ))_k|) from Wang et al. 2021a (7.34), and NTK-based λ*_b = Tr(K_rr)/Tr(K_uu) from Wang et al. 2022b (7.35); for Poisson with K Fourier features λ* ~ K², λ*_a ~ K^{3.5}, λ*_b ~ K⁴, yet the resulting condition numbers κ(A(λ*)) are 'actually very similar'
sampling_strategy: training set S = (S_i, S_s, S_t) = quadrature points: grid-based midpoint/Gauss rules for d ≤ 4, Sobol/Halton low-discrepancy for 4 < d ≤ 20, i.i.d. uniform Monte Carlo for d > 20; separate counts N_int (interior), N_r, N_s in the NS/heat examples; Theorem 6.2 needs N ≥ 2c²ε⁸/(2RΩ)^{n/2} random points for the generalization bound; error vs number of residual points studied empirically (Figs 6.1-6.2)
optimizer_schedule: full gradient descent → SGD → mini-batch with epochs/reshuffling; ADAM with bias correction (2.74)-(2.76); second-order Newton and quasi-Newton (L-BFGS), noted that for linear models the loss Hessian equals A (7.43), relating quasi-Newton to preconditioning; linearized GD converges as (1−c/κ(A))^k, so N(ε) = O(κ(A) ln(1/ε)) steps (7.21); experiment curves shown over 200-2000 epochs (Figs 7.1-7.3)
domain_decomposition: §7.5.4: domain decomposition interpreted as preconditioning — splitting the time domain of the advection equation into N subintervals reduces each subdomain condition number by a factor N² (κ ~ β²), intrinsically connected to causal training of Wang, Sankaran and Perdikaris (2024); Example 5.15: cPINNs (flux continuity for conservation laws) proved stable for Navier-Stokes/advection-diffusion/scalar conservation laws (De Ryck, Jagtap and Mishra 2024b) whereas XPINNs (additional strong-PDE-residual interface terms) were NOT found stable for prototypical PDEs such as Poisson and heat; FBPINN (Moseley et al. 2023) cited as finite-basis decomposition
uq_method: no UQ for PINNs themselves; Gaussian process regression presented as an alternative Bayesian ansatz u_θ ~ GP(m_θ, k_θ) with squared-exponential and Matern covariance kernels (2.38)-(2.40)
data_regime: physics-only (no data) for forward problems; inverse/data-assimilation problems use (possibly noisy) observations Ψ[u]=g on a subdomain Ω′ ⊂ Ω which may exclude the boundary (heat-transfer sensor argument p. 639); numerical illustrations: 1D heat equation on [−1,1], T=1, IC sin(πx) (Fig 6.2); 2D Taylor-Green vortex PINN with ν=0.01 (Fig 6.1); parametric 1D heat IC (6.11); Fourier-feature Poisson/advection examples
datasets_used: no external datasets; model problems: semilinear heat equation; incompressible Navier-Stokes (Taylor-Green vortex with exact solution u,v,p of (6.7)-(6.9) on x,y∈[0.5,4.5]², t∈[0,1], ν=0.01); viscous and inviscid scalar conservation laws; Poisson's equation (1D, incl. toy u=−sin with Dirichlet BCs); linear advection u_t + βu_x = 0 on x∈[0,2π], t∈[0,1]; heat equation with parametric IC u_0(x;μ)=Σ_{i=1}^d (−1/dm²)sin(mπ(x−μ_i)); radiative transfer equation; HJB equations; linear Kolmogorov PDEs (heat, Black-Scholes); Allen-Cahn-type nonlinear parabolic PDE; static Schrödinger equation (Barron regularity)
baselines_compared: classical numerical methods discussed as ansatz-space analogues (spectral/Galerkin/collocation, FEM with h/p/hp refinement, least-squares FEM, finite differences, RBFs); preconditioned vs unpreconditioned Fourier-feature models and MLPs; soft vs hard BC variants; XPINN vs cPINN stability; L²-based vs L^p (p~d) physics loss for HJB (Wang, Li, He and Wang 2022a); DeepONet vs FNO approximation-theory comparison; PINNs vs traditional methods on cost grounds (grid generation, high-dim, inverse problems)
evaluation_metrics: total error E(θ)=||u−u_θ||_{L²(Ω)} (or L¹ for conservation laws, H¹ for variational); generalization error E_G = integral physics-informed loss; training error E_T = J(θ*(S),S); relative generalization percentage error E_G (Fig 6.3); condition number κ(A) of the training matrix; a posteriori and a priori error bounds; convergence rate vs number of residual/training points
key_quantitative_results:
- Error decomposition E* ≤ C(approximation error + generalization gap + optimization error)^α (3.7) organizes the whole survey; Q1-Q4 = existence, stability, generalization, optimization
- A posteriori NS bound (Theorem 6.5): E(θ)² ≤ O(E_T(θ,S) + N_int^{-2/d} + N_r^{-1/(d+1)} + N_s^{-1/d}); total error scales with the SQUARE ROOT of training error, E(θ) ~ √E_T(θ,S), confirmed on Taylor-Green vortex and 1D heat (Figs 6.1-6.2)
- Curse of dimensionality mitigated: heat eq with parametric IC (Fig 6.3) shows E_G grows sub-quadratically (not exponentially) in d, 'Even for very large d the relative generalization error is less than 2%'; PINNs overcome CoD for linear Kolmogorov PDEs (Thm 4.24, width O(poly(d)ρ_d ε^{−(−2+β)/β...})) and Barron-regular Poisson solutions (Thm 7.4: E||u−u_θ||²_{H¹} ≤ C(log N)²/N^{1/3}, rate independent of d)
- Approximation: tanh net, 2 hidden layers width N, ||f−f̂||_{W^{k,∞}} ≤ C(ln(cN))^k N^{−(s−k)/d} (Thm 4.4); BV functions approximated in L¹ by O(ε^{−2})-neuron tanh nets (Lemma 4.16); wPINN entropy-residual bound stays valid for shock solutions (Thm 5.10) while the strong-residual bound blows up as C₁ ~ 1/√ν when viscosity ν→0 (5.18)
- Stability: heat (Thm 5.3), radiative transfer (Thm 5.5), NS (Thm 5.7: ∫||u−u_θ||²dt ≤ Cℰ exp(T(2d²||∇u||_∞+1))), viscous conservation laws (Thm 5.9), Poisson variational (Prop 5.12: E² ≤ 2max{2C_P+1,2}E_G); NEGATIVE result (Thm 5.14, HJB): with L² loss the learned solution can be arbitrarily far from u for high-dim HJB (stability only with L^p, p~d)
- Conditioning (the training bottleneck): Fourier-feature Poisson κ(A_λ) ≥ K⁴ unpreconditioned vs κ̃(A) ≤ C(λ,γ) ≈ 1 preconditioned (Thm 7.12); advection κ(A(β)) ~ β²; soft-BC toy κ = 3+2√2 ≈ 5.83 vs hard-BC variant 1 (multiply η=sin) κ = 4 vs variant 2 (subtract u_θ(π)) κ = 1, so κ(A_hard) < min_λ κ(A_soft); a priori O(ε) NS error attainable if N_r ≥ ε^{−d(1+γ)/(k−γ)}, N_int, N_s scale polynomially in 1/ε (Corollary 7.2)
errors_reported: condition numbers: κ ≥ K⁴ (unpreconditioned Fourier features, Poisson); κ ≈ 1 optimal (preconditioned); κ ~ β² (advection speed β); κ = 3+2√2 ≈ 5.83 (soft BC, optimal λ) vs 4 (hard BC η=sin) vs 1 (hard BC subtract u_θ(π)); relative generalization error < 2% for parametric heat IC even at very large d; error-scaling exponents: E(θ) ~ √E_T; quadrature rates N^{−α} (deterministic) and N^{−1/2}-type Monte Carlo bounds; tanh approximation N^{−(s−k)/d}; BV L¹-approximation O(ε) with O(ε^{−2}) neurons; a priori Poisson/Barron rate (log N)²/N^{1/3}
speedup_claims: no wall-clock speedups vs FEM/FDM claimed; instead: preconditioned Fourier features show loss 'decays exponentially fast' in epochs independent of max frequency K and advection speed β while the unpreconditioned model stalls (Figs 7.1-7.2); FF-MLP loss 'decays much more rapidly' than plain MLP (Fig 7.3); conclusion (p. 706): physics-informed learning is expected to outperform traditional methods on high-dimensional problems, complex geometries (grid generation prohibitive) and inverse problems where data supplements physics
ablations: loss-weighting comparison (Example 7.13: λ*, λ*_a, λ*_b give very similar final condition numbers despite K², K^{3.5}, K⁴ scalings); soft vs hard BC condition-number ablation (§7.5.2, three variants); preconditioned vs unpreconditioned Fourier features (Fig 7.1) and linear advection vs β (Fig 7.2); MLP vs MLP+preconditioned Fourier features spectrum/loss (Fig 7.3); empirical E vs E_T vs theoretical bound and vs number of residual points (Figs 6.1-6.2)
stated_limitations: training error identified as THE key bottleneck which 'can adversely affect the overall performance of various models in physics-informed machine learning' (abstract, p. 633; conclusion p. 706); stability is PDE-specific and can fail outright (HJB, Thm 5.14); sufficient regularity of the PDE solution often required, 'although this regularity can be lessened by changing the form of the PDE' (conclusion); upper bounds on the generalization constant c for PINNs/DeepONets 'often depend exponentially on L' (p. 686); a priori wPINN bound limited because available ||u*||_{C¹} bounds are overestimates growing with ε^{−1} (p. 694); strong-residual stability breaks down for low viscosity/discontinuous solutions (pp. 678-679); for Barron results the constant C 'might depend on the Barron norm of u, and its dependence on d might therefore not be exactly clear' (p. 693)
failure_modes: training with gradient descent can be 'slow, even infeasible', non-converging or converging to unacceptable losses (Krishnapriyan et al. 2021, Moseley et al. 2023, Markham and Nissen-Meyer 2023, Wang et al. 2021a, Wang, Yu and Perdikaris 2022b); non-convex loss landscape; spectral bias of neural networks (Rahaman et al. 2019); subtle imbalance between PDE-residual and supervised loss components diagnosed via infinite-width NTK theory (Wang et al. 2021a; Wang, Wang and Perdikaris 2022b); operator A∘TT* 'very poorly conditioned for most PDEs of practical interest' (κ ≥ K⁴ Fourier features, ~β² advection); exploding/vanishing gradients from bad initialization (§2.5.1); L²-based loss unstable for high-dimensional HJB (Thm 5.14); XPINN instability for prototypical PDEs (Ex 5.15); aliasing errors when discrete FNOs fail to be operators (Bartolucci et al. 2023, motivating ReNOs); weak solutions non-unique for conservation laws without entropy conditions
reproducibility: open-access article (CC BY 4.0, Cambridge University Press); no code or data repository stated; figures reproduced from De Ryck et al. 2024a (IMA J. Numer. Anal., with permission of the IMA) and Molinaro (2023, ETH PhD thesis)
quotable_finding: We identify training errors as a key bottleneck which can adversely affect the overall performance of various models in physics-informed machine learning. (p. 633)
relevance_rqs: RQ2: provides the unified component taxonomy of PINN pipelines (ansatz spaces, strong/weak/variational losses, quadrature/sampling, optimizers, loss weighting) each with theory; RQ3: physics enforcement analysed across residual forms and soft-vs-hard BCs, plus the key mechanism insight that training difficulty is the conditioning of the Hermitian-square operator L*L composed with the tangent-kernel operator, i.e. preconditioning is the unifying fix; RQ4: the central reliability reference — error decomposition, stability guarantees and counterexamples (HJB, XPINN), training-failure diagnosis, and practitioner guidance on when PINNs beat traditional methods (high-dim, complex geometry, inverse)
manuscript_section: S4 methods (enforcement mechanisms, loss design, weighting, optimizers/preconditioning subsections); T2/T3 theory-and-reliability table (error estimates, stability results, negative results); discussion of training bottleneck (can source a dedicated figure on condition numbers)
cross_paper_links: builds-on: PINN-A01 (Raissi, Perdikaris and Karniadakis 2019 modern PINNs; Raissi and Karniadakis 2018 hidden physics), PINN-B07 (XPINN, Jagtap and Karniadakis 2020 - stability counterexample; cPINN Jagtap, Kharazmi and Karniadakis 2020 - proven stable), PINN-B12 (DeepONet Lu et al. 2021a; error estimates via De Ryck and Mishra 2022b), PINN-B13 (FNO Li et al. 2021; ReNO Bartolucci et al. 2023); compares-to: Mishra and Molinaro 2020-2023 error-estimate series, E and Yu 2018 deep Ritz, Kharazmi et al. 2019/2021 VPINN and hp-VPINN, De Ryck, Mishra and Molinaro 2024c wPINN, Krishnapriyan et al. 2021 (PINN failure modes / advection β), Wang et al. 2021a learning-rate annealing, PINN-A06-line NTK works (Wang, Wang and Perdikaris 2022b loss balancing; Liu, Zhu and Belkin 2020), Wang, Sankaran and Perdikaris 2024 causal training, Moseley et al. 2023 FBPINN, Lu, Lu and Wang 2021c Barron-space a priori deep-Ritz bound, De Ryck, Bonnet, Mishra and de Bézenac 2023 operator preconditioning (the survey's backbone for Section 7); De Ryck and Jagtap and Mishra 2024b cPINN/XPINN stability; Grossmann PINN-vs-FEM comparison (PINN-A13) is NOT part of this survey's scope
notes_caveats: Theory-first review, not an application paper: all numerical illustrations are small model problems (1D-2D, periodic/rectangular domains, Taylor-Green vortex), and several conditioning experiments use linear Fourier-feature models rather than full PINNs; a priori bounds certify existence with constants that can be pessimistic (exponential depth-dependence, unclear d-dependence of Barron constants), so they do not translate directly into practical accuracy guarantees; the durable takeaways for our survey are (i) the approximation/stability/generalization/optimization error decomposition, (ii) stability can FAIL (HJB L² loss; XPINN), (iii) training is the bottleneck and its cause is operator ill-conditioning treatable by preconditioning (feature rescaling, hard BCs, second-order optimizers, domain decomposition/causal training); no code released; ~167 citations undercounts influence since its 2024 Acta Numerica status makes it a standard reference
